title: Quantum-Level Crosstalk Characterization of a 16x16 MEMS Optical Switch for Dynamic Quantum Communications
authors: Persefoni Konteli, Nikolas Makris, Grigoris Anastasiou, Konstantinos Tsimvrakidis, George T. Kanellos
abstract: We present an all-to-all quantum-level crosstalk characterization of a commercial 16x16 MEMS optical switch for multi-user quantum communications using SNSPDs, correlating experimental data with a theoretical impact analysis on the decoy-state BB84 QKD protocol.
summary: The paper characterizes the quantum crosstalk noise generated by a commercial 16x16 MEMS optical switch when used for multi-user quantum communications. By measuring photon leakage and correlating this with the decoy-state BB84 QKD protocol, the authors demonstrate that while some port combinations suffer severe noise, the majority are compatible with maintaining high key rates even under significant channel attenuation.
main_problem: The study characterizes quantum-level crosstalk introduced by commercial MEMS optical switches, which poses a potential limitation for implementing robust Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) networks.
main_result: Most port configurations of the 16x16 MEMS switch are found to be compatible with quantum communication, supporting link budgets up to 20 dB, suggesting practical viability for dynamic QKD systems.
method: The authors performed systematic experimental measurements of photon leakage across all input-to-output combinations using SNSPDs and correlated these empirical results with theoretical impact analyses on the decoy-state BB84 protocol.
model_or_system: The platform is a commercial 16x16 MEMS Optical Low-Loss Switch (LLOS) used in conjunction with Superconducting Nanowire Single Photon Detectors (SNSPDs) for quantum signal detection. The analysis focuses on the performance of the decoy-state BB84 QKD protocol.
key_observables: Crosstalk (photon leakage) measured in counts per second ($	ext{cps}$), Secret Key Rate ($	ext{SKR}$) degradation percentage, and Link Loss/Attenuation levels.
important_parameters: Link budgets up to $20 	ext{ dB}$; specific noise thresholds corresponding to $	ext{SKR}$ degradation at $-3 	ext{ dB}$, $-10 	ext{ dB}$, and $-20 	ext{ dB}$.
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes the use of a C-band CW tunable laser source at $1550.12 	ext{ nm}$ and relies on the established framework of the decoy-state BB84 protocol for performance evaluation.
figures_summary: Fig. 1 shows the experimental setup; Fig. 2 displays non-uniform noise counts across port combinations; Fig. 3 presents the ECDF comparing measured crosstalk against simulated $	ext{SKR}$ degradation thresholds for various channel losses.
paper_structure: The paper introduces the problem of classical component crosstalk in quantum networks, details the experimental setup and measurement process (sweeping laser signals), presents the quantitative results showing non-uniform leakage patterns, and concludes with a theoretical impact analysis confirming overall compatibility up to 20 dB attenuation.
why_interesting: This work directly addresses the engineering challenges of integrating macro-scale classical optical components into delicate quantum communication systems, providing crucial empirical data for network feasibility studies in quantum information science.

figures.caption: Fig. 1. The LLOS quantum-level crosstalk characterization setup.

Fig. 2: Noise counts obtained for all classical input–output port combinations of a single quantum channel. The x- and y-axes represent the classical output and input ports, respectively, while the z-axis indicates the corresponding photon noise counts. Figures (a)–(c) illustrate different observed patterns, highlighting the non-uniform distribution of crosstalk-induced noise across the MEMS switch.

Fig. 3. ECDF of the measured crosstalk noise counts across all input–output port combinations. The curve represents the cumulative percentage of port combinations with noise counts below a given value. The markers denote simulated noise thresholds corresponding to SKR degradation levels of −3 dB, −10 dB, and −20 dB for baseline quantum channel losses of 10 dB (black color symbols) and 20 dB (magenta color symbols).
